recipes.title: Santa Maria Grilled Tri-Tip
recipes.blurb: Central California barbecue at its simplest: salt, pepper, garlic, and a hot fire. Tri-tip has a beefy, almost mineral flavor and slices into thin, juicy fans if you read the grain right.

items: 1 tri-tip roast (2½ to 3 lb / 1.1 to 1.4 kg), fat cap trimmed to ¼ in (6 mm)

instructions.title: Trim and inspect the roast
instructions.text: Trim the fat cap down to about ¼ inch (6 mm) and remove any silverskin, which is the thin, shiny membrane that never renders and turns rubbery. Notice the shape: a tri-tip is a triangle with a thick end and a thin tail, which is why the tail always cooks faster. Pat it completely dry before seasoning.

instructions.title: Mix the Santa Maria rub
instructions.text: Stir together the kosher salt, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, crumbled rosemary, and cayenne in a small bowl. Traditional Santa Maria rub is nothing but salt, pepper, and garlic, and the rest here is a light modern touch. Coarse pepper is important — it forms a crust rather than dissolving in.

instructions.title: Season and let it rest
instructions.text: Coat the tri-tip on all sides with the rub, pressing it in firmly with your hands so it adheres. Let it sit on a rack at room temperature for 1 hour, or refrigerate uncovered for up to 24 hours for a deeper dry brine. You will see the surface go from dry to wet to tacky as the salt does its work — tacky is when it is ready.

instructions.title: Build a two-zone fire
instructions.text: For charcoal, bank a full chimney of lit coals to one side; for gas, light half the burners on high and leave the other half off. Close the lid and let the grill settle so the indirect side reads about 350°F (175°C). Red oak is the traditional Santa Maria wood, and a couple of chunks on the coals is a genuine upgrade if you can find it.

instructions.title: Start on the cool side
instructions.text: Brush the tri-tip with the 2 tsp oil and set it on the indirect side, fat cap up, with the thin tail pointed away from the fire. Close the lid and cook for 20 to 30 minutes without opening it. Keeping the thin end away from the heat is how you avoid a well-done tail attached to a rare center.

instructions.title: Cook to 115°F
instructions.text: Start checking at 20 minutes with an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part of the roast. Continue until it reads 115°F (46°C), which usually takes 25 to 35 minutes total at 350°F. Grill temperatures vary a lot, so the thermometer decides when to move on, not the clock.

instructions.title: Sear over direct heat
instructions.text: Move the roast directly over the coals and sear 2 to 3 minutes per side, rotating as needed to build an even dark crust. Expect flare-ups from the rendering fat cap — slide the meat to a cooler spot for a few seconds rather than fighting the flames. The rub will darken noticeably, which is exactly what you want.

instructions.title: Check the final temperature
instructions.text: Pull the tri-tip when the thickest part reads 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare or 138°F (59°C) for medium. Remember that the thin tail will already be 10 to 15 degrees hotter, which is convenient if you are feeding people who like different doneness. Anything past 145°F (63°C) makes this cut noticeably chewy.

instructions.title: Rest 15 minutes
instructions.text: Move the roast to a cutting board and rest it uncovered for 15 minutes. This is a big, dense piece of meat and needs the full time for the juices to settle back into the fibers. Do not tent it tightly with foil, which will steam the crust you just built.

instructions.title: Find where the grain changes
instructions.text: Look closely at the surface: a tri-tip has two muscle groups whose fibers run in different directions, meeting roughly at the middle of the triangle. Cut the roast in half along that line first, separating the two sections. This one step is what separates good tri-tip from tough tri-tip, and almost everybody gets it wrong the first time.

instructions.title: Slice each half against its grain
instructions.text: Turn each half so its fibers run left to right, then slice across them at a slight angle, about ¼ inch (6 mm) thick. You will notice the two halves need to be turned differently, which is the whole point of separating them. Fan the slices out on a warm platter and pour the board juices over the top.

instructions.title: Serve family style
instructions.text: Santa Maria style means the meat goes on the table on a big board and everyone builds their own plate, so put out whatever sides you have made — pinquito or pinto beans, grilled garlic bread, and a fresh salsa are the traditional three. Serve immediately while the slices are hot and the crust is still crisp. Any leftovers should be kept in a whole unsliced piece and cut to order, because sliced beef dries out in the fridge within a day.

tips: This works in the oven too: 350°F (175°C) until 115°F (46°C) internal, roughly 30 to 40 minutes, then sear in a screaming-hot cast-iron skillet for 90 seconds a side.
Tri-tip is common in the western United States and harder to find elsewhere; ask the butcher for a bottom sirloin triangle roast and they will know what you mean.
The dry rub can be mixed in a big batch and stored in a jar for 6 months — it is excellent on steaks, chicken, and potatoes.
Do not slice the whole roast at once if you are not serving it all. Sliced beef dries out within minutes on a platter.
If you cannot find red oak, a chunk of hickory or a couple of soaked oak chips in a foil packet will get you close.
recipes.keyTemp: Move to the sear at 115°F (46°C), then pull off the grill at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare — that is a pull temperature. Carryover adds 3 to 5°F (2 to 3°C) over the 15-minute rest, finishing at 133 to 135°F (56 to 57°C). Above 145°F (63°C) tri-tip gets tough.
recipes.pairing: Pinquito beans, grilled garlic bread, and a big Zinfandel.

recipes.title: Hanger Steak with Chimichurri
recipes.blurb: The butcher's cut, seared hard and drowned in a sharp green herb sauce. Hanger has more flavor than almost anything on the animal, and chimichurri cuts straight through the richness.

items: 1¾ lb (800 g) hanger steak, center sinew removed, in 2 lobes
1 tbsp (15 ml) neutral oil such as grapeseed
1 cup (60 g) finely chopped flat-leaf parsley, packed
2 tbsp finely chopped fresh oregano (or 2 tsp dried)
4 garlic cloves, very finely minced (about 1½ tbsp)
½ tsp (1 g) red pepper flakes
¼ cup (60 ml) red wine vinegar
⅔ cup (160 ml) extra-virgin olive oil
½ tsp (1 g) freshly ground black pepper

instructions.title: Make the chimichurri first
instructions.text: Combine the parsley, oregano, garlic, shallot, and red pepper flakes in a bowl, then stir in the red wine vinegar and the 1 tsp salt. Let that sit for 10 minutes before adding the oil — the vinegar takes the raw bite off the garlic and shallot in that time. Chop everything by hand rather than using a food processor, which bruises the herbs into a dark paste.

instructions.title: Finish and rest the sauce
instructions.text: Whisk in the ⅔ cup olive oil and the ½ tsp black pepper. It should be loose and spoonable, more herbs than liquid, not a smooth emulsion. Let it sit at room temperature for at least 20 minutes while you cook, and taste it again before serving — chimichurri changes noticeably as it sits.

instructions.title: Trim the hanger steak
instructions.text: A hanger steak is two lobes joined by a thick line of sinew down the middle. If your butcher has not already done it, run a boning knife down each side of that sinew to release two long, roughly cylindrical pieces. That center line is inedible and will not soften with cooking, so it has to come out.

instructions.title: Season and temper
instructions.text: Pat the lobes completely dry and season them all over with the 1½ tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp black pepper. Let them sit at room temperature for 20 minutes; hanger is thick and irregular, so tempering matters. Dry them one more time right before they hit the pan.

instructions.title: Heat the skillet hard
instructions.text: Set a 12-inch (30 cm) cast-iron skillet over high heat for 4 to 5 minutes, then add the tablespoon of oil and swirl it. Wait for the first wisp of smoke, around 450°F (230°C). Hanger is coarse-grained and needs an aggressive sear to develop the crust that balances its very beefy flavor.

instructions.title: Sear the first side
instructions.text: Lay the lobes in the pan with space between them and sear undisturbed for 3 minutes. It should sizzle loudly and steadily, not sputter quietly. If your pan is not big enough for both pieces with room to spare, cook them one at a time — crowding is the fastest way to lose your crust.

instructions.title: Turn and build color all around
instructions.text: Because hanger is roughly cylindrical, turn the lobes a quarter turn every 90 seconds to brown all four sides, 5 to 7 minutes total after the first side. Use tongs and lean the pieces against the pan wall if they will not stay put. The goal is even brown color all the way around, not a crust on two sides only.

instructions.title: Check the temperature
instructions.text: Slide a thermometer lengthwise into the thickest lobe and pull the steak at 125 to 128°F (52 to 53°C) for medium-rare. Hanger is one cut you genuinely should not take past medium — the coarse grain that makes it so flavorful also makes it tough and livery when overcooked. If a piece is thinner, pull it earlier and let it rest longer.

instructions.title: Rest on a board
instructions.text: Move the steaks to a cutting board and rest 8 to 10 minutes uncovered. Hanger has a loose grain and releases juice readily, so this rest does real work. Do not wrap it in foil, which will steam away the crust you just built.

instructions.title: Slice against the very obvious grain
instructions.text: Hanger has the most visible grain of any steak — long, coarse fibers running the length of each lobe. Slice across them at a sharp angle into ¼-inch (6 mm) pieces so each slice shows a wide, marbled face. Cutting with the grain here produces something genuinely difficult to chew.

instructions.title: Sauce and serve
instructions.text: Fan the slices on a warm platter, spoon about half the chimichurri over the top, and put the rest in a bowl on the table. The sauce should pool a little and run into the meat, so do not be shy with it. Serve immediately, while the steak is still warm enough to melt slightly into the oil.

tips: Chimichurri keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days and is better after a few hours. Bring it back to room temperature before serving or the olive oil will be cloudy and thick.
Skirt, flank, or flat iron all substitute directly for hanger; adjust the searing time to their thickness and use the same pull temperature.
If your butcher does not carry hanger, ask ahead — there is only one per animal, which is why it used to be the cut butchers took home.
Do not skip the 10-minute vinegar soak for the garlic and shallot. Raw garlic straight into oil stays harsh and can overwhelm the herbs.
Leftover chimichurri is excellent on eggs, roasted potatoes, grilled chicken, and crusty bread.
recipes.keyTemp: Pull at 125 to 128°F (52 to 53°C) for medium-rare — that is a pull temperature, taken out of the pan. Carryover adds about 5°F (3°C) during the 8- to 10-minute rest, finishing at 130 to 133°F (54 to 56°C). Hanger becomes tough and livery past 140°F (60°C).
recipes.pairing: Blistered shishito peppers and roasted potatoes, with a Malbec.

recipes.title: Steak Frites with Herb Butter
recipes.blurb: Twice-fried French fries and a seared steak under a melting disc of maitre d'hotel butter. The double fry is the whole secret, and once you have done it you will never bake a fry again.

items: 2 lb (900 g) russet potatoes, about 3 large
2 qt (2 L) peanut or canola oil, for frying
1½ tsp (7 g) fine sea salt, for finishing
2 New York strip or sirloin steaks (10 oz / 285 g each, 1¼ in / 3 cm thick)
¼ tsp (1 g) freshly ground black pepper

instructions.title: Make the herb butter
instructions.text: Mash the softened butter with the parsley, lemon juice, ½ tsp salt, and ¼ tsp pepper until evenly combined. Roll it into a log in plastic wrap about 1¼ inches (3 cm) across and refrigerate at least 30 minutes until firm. Cold butter melts slowly over the hot steak instead of instantly flooding the plate.

instructions.title: Cut the potatoes evenly
instructions.text: Peel the russets and square off the sides, then cut them into batons about ⅜ inch (1 cm) thick and as close to the same size as you can manage. Uneven fries cook unevenly, so the thin ones burn while the thick ones stay raw inside. Russets are essential here — their high starch and low moisture is what makes a fluffy interior possible.

instructions.title: Soak away the surface starch
instructions.text: Put the cut potatoes in a bowl of cold water and let them soak for 30 minutes, changing the water once if it clouds heavily. This rinses off loose surface starch that would otherwise make the fries stick together and turn gummy. Drain them and dry them thoroughly on kitchen towels — water and hot oil is a dangerous combination.

instructions.title: Set up the fryer safely
instructions.text: Pour the oil into a heavy 6-quart pot until it comes no more than a third of the way up the sides, and clip on a deep-fry thermometer. Never fill past a third; oil expands and foams violently when wet potatoes go in. Keep a lid and a box of baking soda nearby, and never use water on an oil fire.

instructions.title: First fry at 325°F
instructions.text: Heat the oil to 325°F (163°C) and fry the potatoes in three batches for 5 to 6 minutes each, until they are soft and pale blond but not browned. Move them with a spider to a paper-towel-lined rack. The first fry is about cooking the inside through, not color, so resist the urge to leave them longer.

instructions.title: Rest the fries
instructions.text: Let the blanched fries rest at room temperature for at least 20 minutes, or refrigerate them for up to 4 hours. This rest lets the surface dry and the interior set, which is why twice-fried fries stay crisp far longer than single-fried ones. Meanwhile, let the oil come back to temperature and season your steaks.

instructions.title: Season and temper the steaks
instructions.text: Pat the steaks completely dry and season on both sides and the edges with the 1½ tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp black pepper. Leave them at room temperature for 20 to 30 minutes so the centers are not fridge-cold. Get a cast-iron skillet heating on a second burner over medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes.

instructions.title: Sear the steaks
instructions.text: Add the tablespoon of oil to the hot skillet, wait for the shimmer, and lay the steaks in away from you. Sear 3½ to 4 minutes on the first side and 3 minutes on the second, then stand them on their fat edge for 30 seconds. You want an aggressive, steady sizzle the whole time and a deep brown crust when you flip.

instructions.title: Pull and rest the steaks
instructions.text: Check the center with an instant-read thermometer and pull at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare or 135°F (57°C) for medium. Move them to a cutting board and rest 8 to 10 minutes while you finish the fries. Steak reheats badly, so the timing here matters: the steak rests exactly as long as the second fry takes.

instructions.title: Second fry at 375°F
instructions.text: Raise the oil to 375°F (190°C) and fry the rested potatoes in batches for 2 to 3 minutes each, until deep golden and audibly crisp when you stir them. Do not crowd the pot — too many at once drops the temperature and gives you greasy, limp fries. Let the oil come back to 375°F between batches.

instructions.title: Salt the fries immediately
instructions.text: Drain each batch onto a rack or paper towels and season right away with the fine sea salt while the surface is still glistening with oil. Salt only sticks in that first 20 seconds; add it later and it slides straight off. Toss them in a bowl so they season evenly.

instructions.title: Plate and serve at once
instructions.text: Set each steak on a warm plate, top with a ½-inch (1 cm) coin of the herb butter, and pile the frites alongside in a tall heap. Pour any board juices over the meat. This is a dish that waits for nobody — get it to the table while the fries are still crackling and the butter is only half melted.

tips: Do the first fry up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate the blanched fries. That turns this from a juggling act into a very manageable dinner.
A deep-fry or instant-read thermometer is genuinely required. Oil that is too cool gives you greasy fries; too hot and they brown before the inside cooks.
Peanut oil has the highest smoke point and the cleanest flavor, but canola works fine. Strain and reuse the cooled oil two or three times.
If you only have one burner free, fry first and keep the fries warm on a rack in a 200°F (95°C) oven, then sear the steaks last.
Maitre d'hotel butter freezes for 3 months; slice coins off the frozen log straight onto hot steak, fish, or vegetables.
recipes.keyTemp: Steak: 125°F (52°C) is a pull temperature — carryover over the 8- to 10-minute rest brings it to 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium-rare. Oil: 325°F (163°C) for the first fry, 375°F (190°C) for the second.
recipes.pairing: A simple butter-lettuce salad with mustard vinaigrette, and a cold Belgian-style beer or a Côtes du Rhône.

recipes.title: Prime Rib Roast with Au Jus
recipes.blurb: A standing rib roast cooked low and slow, then blasted at the end for a crackling crust. This is the holiday centerpiece, and the low-oven method makes it almost impossible to overcook.

items: 1 bone-in standing rib roast, 3 to 4 ribs (7 to 8 lb / 3.2 to 3.6 kg)
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, about ¾ tsp per pound of meat
1 tbsp chopped fresh rosemary and 1 tbsp chopped fresh thyme
½ cup (120 ml) dry red wine or dry sherry
3 sprigs fresh thyme and 1 bay leaf
½ tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste

instructions.title: Dry brine 24 to 48 hours ahead
instructions.text: Pat the roast completely dry and rub it all over with the 2 tbsp kosher salt, including the ends and between the bones. Set it on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for 24 to 48 hours. This is the most important step in the recipe: it seasons the interior, dries the surface for a better crust, and there is no shortcut that gets you the same result.

instructions.title: Temper the roast
instructions.text: Take the roast out of the fridge exactly 2 hours before it goes in the oven and leave it on the counter, uncovered, on its rack. Two hours is the ceiling, not a suggestion — raw beef should never sit at room temperature longer than that, because the surface is where bacteria live and it warms first. A cold 8-pound roast can add well over an hour of cooking time and will cook far less evenly, so this window is worth using fully. If your kitchen runs hot, above about 80°F (27°C), cut it to 1 hour.

instructions.title: Make the herb paste
instructions.text: Mash the softened butter with the chopped rosemary, thyme, black pepper, and garlic powder into a rough paste. Smear it over the fat cap and the exposed meat ends, but not the bones. The butter helps the herbs adhere and browns into the crust during the final blast.

instructions.title: Set the roasting pan
instructions.text: Scatter the quartered onion and carrot pieces across the bottom of a roasting pan and set the roast on top, bone-side down, so the bones act as a natural rack. If you have a wire rack, use it and put the vegetables underneath. Insert a leave-in probe thermometer into the very center of the eye, avoiding bone and fat seams.

instructions.title: Roast low at 250°F
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 250°F (120°C) and roast, uncovered, until the center hits 118 to 120°F (48 to 49°C) for medium-rare. Plan on roughly 25 to 30 minutes per pound, so about 3½ to 4 hours for an 8-pound roast, but check early. A low oven cooks the meat evenly edge to edge instead of leaving a thick gray band under the crust.

instructions.title: Trust the thermometer, not the clock
instructions.text: Start checking at the 2½-hour mark, and every 20 minutes after that. Roast weight, bone-in versus boneless, oven calibration, and starting temperature all swing the timing by an hour or more. For medium, take it to 128°F (53°C); the final crust blast will add about 5 to 10°F (3 to 6°C) on top of whatever it reads now.

instructions.title: Rest the roast, uncovered
instructions.text: Pull the roast out, transfer it to a carving board, and let it rest 30 to 45 minutes while the oven heats up. It will hold its heat easily — a roast this size loses only a few degrees in that window. Leave it uncovered so the surface stays dry for the crust step.

instructions.title: Build the jus base
instructions.text: Set the roasting pan with its vegetables over two burners on medium heat, skim off all but 2 tablespoons of fat, and pour in the ½ cup wine. Scrape the pan hard with a wooden spoon to lift every browned bit and let it reduce by half, about 3 minutes. Add the 3 cups beef stock, thyme sprigs, and bay leaf and simmer 12 to 15 minutes.

instructions.title: Blast the oven for the crust
instructions.text: Crank the oven to 500°F (260°C) and let it fully preheat, which takes 15 to 20 minutes. Return the rested roast on a clean sheet pan and roast for 6 to 10 minutes, watching closely, until the exterior is deeply browned and crackling. Pull it the moment it looks right; at this temperature it goes from perfect to burnt in about 3 minutes.

instructions.title: Finish the au jus
instructions.text: Strain the jus through a fine-mesh sieve into a small saucepan, pressing the vegetables gently, and discard the solids. Skim any remaining fat off the surface, bring it to a simmer, and whisk in the cold tablespoon of butter until glossy. Taste and add the ½ tsp salt as needed — jus should be intensely beefy and thin, not thick like gravy.

instructions.title: Carve off the bones
instructions.text: Stand the roast on end and run a long knife down between the meat and the rib bones, following the curve, to release the whole eye in one piece. Cut the bone rack into individual ribs for anyone at the table who wants one, because they are the best part. Set the boneless roast flat on the board.

instructions.title: Slice and serve
instructions.text: Slice the roast across the grain into ½- to ¾-inch (1 to 2 cm) thick pieces, keeping the crust attached to each slice. Serve on warm plates with the au jus in a pitcher alongside and any board juices poured over. Prime rib cools fast, so warm the plates and get everyone seated before you start carving.

tips: Buy the roast a few days early so you have time for the 24- to 48-hour dry brine. It is the difference between good prime rib and great prime rib.
Ask the butcher to cut the bones free and tie them back on. You get the flavor and insulation of bone-in, and carving becomes trivially easy.
A leave-in probe thermometer is not optional on a roast this expensive. Opening the oven to check repeatedly costs you both heat and accuracy.
Plan on about 1 pound of bone-in roast per person, or two people per rib. An 8-pound, 4-rib roast comfortably serves 8.
Serve horseradish cream alongside: stir ¼ cup prepared horseradish, ½ cup sour cream, 1 tsp lemon juice, and ¼ tsp salt together and chill for an hour.
recipes.keyTemp: Roast at 250°F (120°C) and pull at 118 to 120°F (48 to 49°C) for medium-rare — a pull temperature, well short of where you want to eat it. The rest plus the 500°F (260°C) crust blast adds 10 to 14°F (6 to 8°C) of carryover, finishing at 128 to 132°F (53 to 56°C). Medium is 140°F (60°C).
recipes.pairing: Yorkshire puddings, creamed spinach, and a serious Cabernet Sauvignon or Bordeaux.
